content.text:
I'm with a cultural heritage project in Europe, and I want a documentary explainer about a medieval stone arch bridge we've just finished restoring. The accuracy rests entirely on the script I'm giving you — read it as written and don't fill anything in yourself: the date of the bridge, where the stone came from, the several times floods damaged it and the traditional methods we used this time are all in the script, and not a single figure can be changed or added. I'm providing real photo references of the bridge after restoration, and the bridge in the film has to match those exactly — the curve of the arch, the texture of the joints between the stones, those are the real thing. For the narration we had a local craftsman record the commentary in English; use his real human voice, the bit of accent is exactly the texture we want, don't replace it. I'm also attaching a string-music recording we made to sit underneath. The finished piece should be documentary with a light infographic feel, steady in tone. English narration with English subtitles, and fill in chisel and running-water ambience to match what's on screen. The runtime follows the narration audio, around a minute and a half.

Here is the commentary, word for word:

project record; nothing may be changed, rounded, or added.

The Pont de la Roche-Vieille was completed in 1387. It carries a single
segmental arch of twenty-two metres over the Vère, and it has stood for six
hundred and thirty-nine years.

The stone is a local grey limestone, quarried at Saint-Martin-de-Vère, four
kilometres upstream. We went back to the same quarry for this work, so that
every replacement block came out of the same bed as the original.

The river has taken the bridge three times. The flood of 1612 carried away the
eastern parapet. In 1875 the western cutwater was undermined and lost. And in
October 2019 a hundred-year flood opened a crack through the arch ring itself.

We rebuilt it the way it was built. The blocks were dressed by hand with a
point chisel and a bush hammer, no power tools on any visible face. They were
set in a hot-mixed lime mortar, six parts sand to one part quicklime, with no
cement anywhere in the structure. The arch was reset on a timber centring
built on site from green oak.

The work took nineteen months. Four masons, one carpenter, and one
apprentice — who is now a mason.

The bridge is open again. It is expected to stand another six hundred years.
